bigPicture.subtitle: The Treasure God Will Only Trust to a Cracked Jar
paragraphs: Around AD 56, somewhere in Macedonia, a man who by his own account had not had one moment’s relief in months finally picked up a pen. He had written to Corinth before — the long, patient, corrective letter you have just finished. It had not worked. The situation got worse. So he went himself, and that visit went so badly that he can never afterward call it anything but sorrow: “But I determined this for myself, that I would not come to you again in sorrow” (2:1). Then, instead of going back, he wrote. Not this letter — another one, composed in a state he makes no attempt to dress up: “For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears, not that you should be made sorry, but that you might know the love that I have so abundantly for you” (2:4). That severe letter is not in your Bible. God let the earthquake go and kept the aftershock. And then came the waiting — and the waiting is where you meet the real man. He had sent it with Titus, and he could not bear the silence. He got as far as Troas, found a city wide open to the gospel, and walked away from it: “Now when I came to Troas for the Good News of Christ, and when a door was opened to me in the Lord, I had no relief for my spirit, because I didn’t find Titus, my brother, but taking my leave of them, I went out into Macedonia” (2:12–13). The greatest missionary in history abandoned an open door because he could not stop thinking about a church that had hurt him. And when he reached Macedonia it got worse before it got better: “our flesh had no relief, but we were afflicted on every side. Fightings were outside. Fear was inside” (7:5). Then Titus arrived carrying the news that they had repented, that they were grieving, that they wanted him back (7:6–7). Second Corinthians is what a man writes in the first days after that relief, while his hands are still shaking. That is why it swings so violently between joy and grief. He was still bleeding when he wrote it.

While he had been away, teachers had arrived in Corinth carrying letters of recommendation — he mentions them with visible irritation in 3:1 — and they had built a case against him. Paul refers to them, with the driest sarcasm in Scripture, as “the very best apostles” (11:5; 12:11). Behind the English sits ὑπερλίαν, a mash of ὑπέρ (hypér, G5228, “over, beyond”) and λίαν (lían, G3029, “exceedingly”) — the super-apostles, the extra-special ones. When the irony runs out he says what he actually thinks: “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as Christ’s apostles. And no wonder, for even Satan masquerades as an angel of light” (11:13–14). Masquerade is μετασχηματίζω (metaschēmatízō, G3345) — to change the outward shape, to put on a costume. Their charges were three, and all three came down to one verdict, delivered in the letter’s own vocabulary: the man carries no weight. First, he did not look the part: “His letters,” they say, “are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (10:10). Second, he was unreliable — he had changed his travel plans, so his yes could not be trusted (1:17). Third — and this one only stings if you understand Corinth — he had refused their money: “Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself that you might be exalted, because I preached to you God’s Good News free of charge?” (11:7). In a city where teachers were priced like merchandise, a free teacher was a cheap teacher. Now watch what he does with charge number one, because it is the hinge of the entire letter. He never denies it. He does not argue anywhere in thirteen chapters that he is more impressive than they say. He concedes the point — and then builds his whole defence on the very thing they used to disqualify him.

If the only Paul you have met is the Paul of the doctrine chapters — the lawyer of Romans, the systematician, the man with the airtight argument — you have not met the man. This letter is his exposed nerve. He tells them about a season in Asia so crushing that faith was not the question, survival was: “we were weighed down exceedingly, beyond our power, so much that we despaired even of life. Yes, we ourselves have had the sentence of death within ourselves” (1:8–9). Despaired is ἐξαπορέομαι (exaporéomai, G1820) — utterly at a loss, every exit closed. He turns savage: “For you bear with the foolish gladly, being wise. For you bear with a man, if he brings you into bondage, if he devours you, if he takes you captive, if he exalts himself, if he strikes you on the face” (11:19–20) — you will take a slap in the face from a stranger, and you will not take a letter from your father. He turns tender in a way the argument never allows: “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians. Our heart is enlarged” (6:11) — he breaks off and says their name out loud, mid-sentence, like a man reaching across a table — and then asks for it back the only way a father can: “Now in return, I speak as to my children, you also open your hearts” (6:13). He boasts and despises himself for it: “I have become foolish in boasting. You compelled me” (12:11). And near the end he admits he is frightened of his own arrival: “For I am afraid that by any means, when I come, I might find you not the way I want to, and that I might be found by you as you don’t desire” (12:20). Crushed, sarcastic, tender, boasting against his will, and finally almost pleading — that is the emotional range of thirteen chapters. Do not flatten it into a lecture. Read the man.

The letter moves in three movements, and you should know the shape of them before you start. Chapters 1–7 are the ministry of the new covenant: comfort forged inside affliction, the aroma of Christ carried through a Roman triumph, a covenant written not on stone but on hearts, the treasure in clay jars, the ministry of reconciliation — and then, in chapter 7, the tearful reunion with the church itself. Chapters 8–9 are the relief offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem, the most sustained teaching on giving anywhere in the New Testament. Notice where he anchors it. Not in duty, not in percentages, not in guilt, but here: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich” (8:9). Christian giving is downward mobility in imitation of a King who went down first. Chapters 10–13 are the defence of his apostleship, and the tone changes so sharply that some scholars have argued these four chapters were originally a separate letter stitched on later. Be honest about that and move on: no manuscript of 2 Corinthians has ever been found without them, and a man who has just been forgiven is exactly the man who finally turns and says the hard thing he has been holding in his chest for a year. Read it as one letter, written by one exhausted, relieved, still-wounded pastor.

And every road in it runs toward one sentence. Somewhere in his body Paul carried something he calls “a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me” (12:7). Scripture never says what it was — and that silence is a mercy, because the blank was left open so that every reader in every century could write his own name in it. He prayed about it exactly the way you have prayed about yours: “Concerning this thing, I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me” (12:8). Three times. That is not a casual request; that is Gethsemane’s number. And the answer was not yes, and it was not no. It was a third thing that nobody asks for and everybody eventually needs: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (12:9). The despair in Asia, the cracked jar, the catalogue of beatings, the thorn — all of it is laid down like track running to that one line. So know who this book is for before you open chapter 1. It is for the believer who is failing. It is for the one who is tired, who has been humiliated, who is not impressive in a room, who watches more gifted people take the platform, who has quietly concluded that his scars have disqualified him. Second Corinthians exists to tell that man the truth: the scars are the credential.

bridge.intro: The Holy Spirit set 2 Corinthians directly after 1 Corinthians because it is the same pastor writing to the same church — but in the months between the two letters, everything changed:

points.title: The Letter That Is Missing Between These Two
points.body: Do not read 2 Corinthians as though it picks up the next morning. There is roughly a year of wreckage between the last verse of 1 Corinthians and the first verse of this one. The first letter did not fix Corinth; it brought the fight into the open. So Paul went in person, and that visit was a disaster — he can only ever call it sorrow, and he vowed never to repeat it: “But I determined this for myself, that I would not come to you again in sorrow” (2:1). Then he wrote them a letter so severe that he flinched at his own handwriting afterward: “For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears” (2:4). He sent it with Titus and then spent weeks second-guessing it: “For though I made you sorry with my letter, I do not regret it, though I did regret it” (7:8) — a sentence so honest it barely holds together. That severe letter is lost. God did not preserve it, and He did not need to; He preserved what it produced. So when you find tenderness in chapter 7 and fury in chapter 11 inside the same book, you are not reading an inconsistent author. You are reading a man on the far side of a rupture that nearly cost him a church he had fathered.

points.title: From the Chair to the Chest
points.body: In 1 Corinthians Paul writes with an authority he simply assumes. Do this. Stop that. Don’t you know? He can close a whole section by asking, almost casually, “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Corinthians 4:21) — a father with the belt still hanging on the wall and no doubt whatever about his right to use it. Turn the page into this letter and that same man opens his defence like this: “Now I Paul, myself, entreat you by the humility and gentleness of Christ; I who in your presence am lowly among you, but being absent am bold toward you” (10:1). He is not instructing from a settled chair anymore. He is opening his chest. You can see the same movement even in how he handles discipline. In the first letter he ordered a sinning man put out of the assembly (1 Corinthians 5:4–5, 13). In this one he pleads for a disciplined man to be brought back in: “so that on the contrary you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you to confirm your love toward him” (2:7–8) — and he gives a reason every church that loves discipline more than people needs nailed to its door: “that no advantage may be gained over us by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his schemes” (2:11). (Whether that man is the offender of 1 Corinthians 5 or someone who attacked Paul during the painful visit is genuinely debated — the letter’s own distinction in 7:12 between “his cause that did the wrong” and “his cause that suffered the wrong” leans toward the second. The pastoral principle is identical either way.) A father correcting his children has become a father showing them his scars. Neither posture is weakness. Both are love.

points.title: The Sermon He Preached Them, Now Preached in His Body
points.body: First Corinthians measured everything by the cross and told a status-obsessed city the most offensive thing you can say to people who are climbing: “God chose the weak things of the world, that he might put to shame the things that are strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27), so “that no flesh should boast before God” (1:29), and he sealed it with a line borrowed from Jeremiah: “He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (1:31). That was theology preached at them. Now watch what happens when God takes that identical theology and proves it in the preacher’s own body. Paul quotes Jeremiah again in this letter, the same sentence in the same words — “But ‘he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord’” (10:17) — except that this time he has a thorn he cannot pray away, a body they call weak and a voice they call despised. And he says: “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness” (11:30). What he taught them in the first letter, he now lives in front of them in the second. The Lord’s answer in 12:9 is nothing less than the doctrine of 1 Corinthians 1 spoken back to Paul as a personal word: my power is made perfect in weakness. That is how God usually teaches. He gives you the sentence first. Then, years later, He gives you the circumstances that make you believe it.

points.title: The Two Open Doors
points.body: Here is the detail that measures the distance between these two letters, and it hides in plain sight because Paul uses the same picture in both. At the end of 1 Corinthians he explains why he is staying put in Ephesus rather than coming to them: “for a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries” (1 Corinthians 16:9). An open door — so he stayed, adversaries and all, because opportunity outranked comfort. Now watch the same man at Troas a year later: “when a door was opened to me in the Lord, I had no relief for my spirit, because I didn’t find Titus, my brother, but taking my leave of them, I went out into Macedonia” (2:12–13). Same picture. Same God. Same opportunity. And this time he walked away from it — because a church that had wounded him was still on his heart, and he could not preach while he did not know whether they were all right. Somewhere in that year, love got heavier than opportunity. If you want a single measurement of the distance from 1 Corinthians to 2 Corinthians, it is those two doors: the one he stayed for, and the one he could not walk through.

coreTheme.title: My Grace Is Sufficient for You, for My Power Is Made Perfect in Weakness
paragraphs: The whole letter has one gravitational centre, and Paul only reaches it after he has been humiliated into talking about himself. He mentions, in the third person, as though it happened to somebody else, that fourteen years earlier he was “caught up into the third heaven” and “caught up into Paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (12:2, 4). He will not describe it. Then he tells you the price tag: “By reason of the exceeding greatness of the revelations, that I should not be exalted excessively, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me, that I should not be exalted excessively” (12:7). Thorn is σκόλοψ (skólops, G4647) — not a splinter in a fingertip but a stake, something sharpened at the end and driven in. Torment is κολαφίζω (kolaphízō, G2852): to strike with the fist. Not an inconvenience — a beating, repeated, on a schedule. And read the grammar carefully: it was given. Satan is the fist, but the verb is passive and the purpose is holy, which means the messenger of Satan is on a leash, and God is holding the other end. So Paul did what you have done: “Concerning this thing, I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me. He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness’” (12:8–9).

Every word of that answer is loaded. Sufficient is ἀρκέω (arkéō, G714), and Christ speaks it in the present tense — not it will be sufficient when this is finally over, but it is sufficing you now, in the middle, while the fist is still landing. Made perfect is τελειόω (teleióō, G5048): to bring a thing all the way to completion, to consummate it, to finish it off at its intended end. Weakness is ἀσθένεια (asthéneia, G769) — feebleness of body or mind, frailty, the state of having no strength left. Power is δύναμις (dýnamis, G1411). Put them together and you have a sentence that reverses everything you were ever taught about how strength works: God’s power does not merely tolerate your weakness — it reaches its designed completion there. Then look at what Paul says back, because the image inside it is stunning: “Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me” (12:9). Rest on is ἐπισκηνόω (episkēnóō, G1981) — to pitch a tent upon, to tabernacle over. It is the vocabulary of the glory settling on the tent in the wilderness. And seven chapters earlier Paul had already called your body a tent — σκῆνος (skēnos, G4636): “if the earthly house of our tent is dissolved” (5:1). So here is the picture the Greek is painting for you. Your tent is fraying. And precisely over the fraying place, the glory of God pitches His tent. The crack is not the obstacle to the glory. The crack is the doorway.

This is not a special arrangement God improvised for one apostle. It is how He has always worked, and the Old Testament is a long series of rehearsals for 12:9. God took Gideon’s army from thirty-two thousand men down to three hundred, and stated His reason plainly — so that Israel could never turn around and claim the victory as its own — and then had those three hundred hide their torches inside clay jars, so that the light only broke over the valley in the moment the jars were smashed (Judges 7). Jacob wrestled all night, won a new name, and walked away from the encounter limping for the rest of his life; the blessing and the limp arrived in the same instant (Genesis 32). Moses’ great objection to his calling was his own mouth (Exodus 4:10) — and God chose him anyway, and never fixed the mouth. Then the principle comes to a head at Calvary, where Paul states it in its purest form: “For he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (13:4). Read that twice. God did not invent this rule for your comfort, and He did not invent it for Paul. He proved it on His own Son first — the most total weakness in the history of the universe, a naked man nailed to a beam and buried in a borrowed grave — and out of it came the resurrection. The cross is 2 Corinthians 12:9 written in blood. Every time God’s power has broken into this world at full strength, it has come through something that first looked like defeat.

So the sentence detonates across the entire book. “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (4:7). “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (6:10). “Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong” (12:10). And it has never stopped detonating. Fanny Crosby was blinded as an infant and went on to write thousands of hymns the church is still singing more than a century after her death. Amy Carmichael fell in 1931 in south India, spent most of the next twenty years confined to one room, and wrote from that bed the books that sent a generation to the mission field. Neither woman got the thorn removed. Both of them got the grace. Now bring it home, because this is not a museum exhibit. You have a thing you have asked God three times to take away. Hear His answer precisely: He did not say the thorn is good. He did not say stop asking. He said something better and far harder — I am enough for you inside it, and My strength will finish itself in exactly the place where you have none. And notice the tense one more time. ἀρκεῖ is present. Not one day. Today. The grace you are waiting for is not in transit; it has already arrived.

truths.intro: As we journey through these 13 chapters, the Holy Spirit wants to anchor these truths in your spirit:

items.title: God Comforts You Inside the Affliction, Never Instead of It
items.body: The letter opens with a name for God that only a man who has been through something could have written: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort; who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God” (1:3–4). Comfort is παράκλησις (paráklēsis, G3874), from παρακαλέω (parakaléō, G3870) — to call someone alongside. It is not a blanket and a hot drink. It is reinforcement summoned to your side while the pressure is still on you. And affliction is θλῖψις (thlîpsis, G2347), which literally means pressure — the crushing weight of a stone coming down on grapes. Now read the sentence again and notice what Paul never asks for. He does not ask God to lift the θλῖψις. He blesses God for the παράκλησις that arrives inside it. Then catch the purpose clause, because it is the whole point: God comforts you so that you can comfort. What He pours in, He intends to pour through. Your suffering is being converted into currency you will one day spend on somebody else, and the plain truth is that a man who has never been in the pit has nothing to say to the man who is in it. Then Paul tells them how far down he went — “we despaired even of life. Yes, we ourselves have had the sentence of death within ourselves” — and gives God’s stated reason for permitting it: “that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead” (1:8–9). That is the most under-preached line in the chapter. The despair had a design. He was taken past the end of his own resources on purpose, because a man who still has a backup plan has never yet met the God who raises the dead. And it held: “who delivered us out of so great a death, and does deliver; on whom we have set our hope that he will also still deliver us” (1:10). Past, present, future — delivered, delivers, will deliver. Put your name in all three tenses.

items.title: The Treasure Is Real — the Jar Was Always Meant to Crack
items.body: “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (4:7). Treasure is θησαυρός (thēsaurós, G2344) — a deposit of wealth. Vessel is σκεῦος (skeûos, G4632), and clay is ὀστράκινος (ostrákinos, G3749): earthenware, potsherd, the cheapest disposable container in the ancient world. Nobody repaired one; you threw it out and bought another. Exceeding greatness is ὑπερβολή (hyperbolḗ, G5236) — an amount thrown far beyond the normal measure. Put those words side by side and the logic is inescapable: the container is deliberately worthless so that no observer could ever confuse the container with the contents. Remember Gideon’s three hundred, whose torches only lit the valley when the jars were broken. God has not been failing to upgrade you. He has been guarding His own glory. Then Paul describes what life inside a clay jar actually feels like, and it comes as four hammer blows, each one answered by a mercy: “We are pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, yet not to despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed” (4:8–9). Look hard at what God does and does not promise there. He never says you will not be pressed, confused, hunted or floored. He guarantees the second half of every clause. And then he does the accounting: “For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory” (4:17). Weight is βάρος (báros, G922) — the Hebrew mind always heard glory as heaviness, as mass, as something with real substance to it. This is a man who has been beaten with rods three times and stoned once, and he calls all of it light. Not because it did not hurt. Because he has held the other side of the scale in his hands. So stop praying for a better jar. Start praying to be a jar that lets the light out.

items.title: You Have Been Handed the Ministry of Reconciliation — You Are an Ambassador Now
items.body: Chapter 5 holds the densest statement of the gospel in the New Testament outside Romans, and it never stays theoretical for a single verse. “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (5:17). New is καινός (kainós, G2537) — new in kind, not merely new in time; a different sort of thing from what stood there before. Creation is κτίσις (ktísis, G2937), the word for an original act of forming. Then: “But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation” (5:18). Reconciliation is καταλλαγή (katallagḗ, G2643) — an exchange, a difference fully settled, an enmity dealt with at the root; the verb behind it is καταλλάσσω (katallássō, G2644). God did not meet you halfway. He did all the reconciling — and then handed you the job: “We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (5:20). Ambassador is πρεσβεύω (presbeúō, G4243) — to act as the appointed representative of a sovereign in a foreign country: no authority of your own, and the full authority of the One who sent you. And what moves an ambassador who owns nothing? “For the love of Christ constrains us” (5:14) — συνέχω (synéchō, G4912), to press in from both sides, to hem a man in, the word for a crowd squeezing someone so tightly that he can only move in one direction. Then comes the sentence the entire exchange rests on: “For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf; so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (5:21). Sin is ἁμαρτία (hamartía, G266); righteousness is δικαιοσύνη (dikaiosýnē, G1343). He took your category so that you could be given His. And that same downward motion is precisely how Paul will later argue about money — “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich” (8:9) — which is why the giving chapters are not a fundraising appeal but a doctrine of the incarnation applied to a wallet, and why “God loves a cheerful giver” (9:7), ἱλαρός (hilarós, G2431), the root behind our English word hilarious. So settle this now: you are not a spectator of reconciliation. You are carrying it in your mouth — into your family, your workplace and your street, this week.

preparation.intro: Before we step into Chapter 1, prepare your spirit with these reflections:

items.title: The Name You Measure Yourself Against
items.body: Paul says harder things about these rivals than this one — false apostles, deceitful workers (11:13). But the quietest thing he says about them is the line that will do the most damage in your life, because it is the one you are most likely to be guilty of yourself. He says they had lost their minds: “But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding” (10:12). Without understanding — because a ruler made out of other men is not a ruler at all. It is a mirror, and it will tell you whatever you are most afraid of. So do this before you open chapter 1, and be specific enough that it stings. Name the person. Not the category — the person. Who is the believer, the colleague, the sibling, the preacher, the account you keep opening, whose life quietly functions as the measuring line for yours? Write the name somewhere only you will ever see it. Then write beside it the thing they have that you have been treating as evidence that God values them more than you: the gift, the platform, the marriage, the money, the ease, the voice, the body, the results. Now hold both of those against two verses: “But ‘he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.’ For it isn’t he who commends himself who is approved, but whom the Lord commends” (10:17–18). There is exactly one Assessor in this universe, and He has already commended you in Christ. Every hour you spend on that comparison is an hour stolen out of your own assignment. Say it out loud today, by name, and repent of it.

items.title: The Third Prayer
items.body: “Concerning this thing, I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me” (12:8). You have a this thing. Name it before you begin, because you cannot receive this book in the abstract. Is it the illness that has not turned around? The temptation you have confessed so many times that you have stopped believing your own confession? The marriage, the child, the debt, the depression that lifts and returns on a cycle you can almost predict? The limitation you were born with, the failure that is still on your record, the scar you have privately decided disqualifies you from ever being used? Say it plainly to God — not as a complaint, but as a naming. Then sit with the hard question and do not rush past it: if God’s answer to you turns out to be the same answer He gave Paul — grace, and not removal — will you still serve Him? Will you still get up, still give, still open your mouth about Jesus, still love the people who found you unimpressive? And then ask the practical version of it, because a faith that changes nothing on Monday is not faith: what would you actually attempt this month if you truly believed that God’s power is completed in weakness rather than blocked by it? The thing you have never tried because you are not healed enough, gifted enough, qualified enough or eloquent enough — that thing. Write it down. You will need it again when you reach chapter 12.

prayerOfActivation: Father of mercies and God of all comfort, I come into this letter as I actually am, not as I pretend to be. You know the affliction I am carrying, and You know how long I have been asking You to remove it. Before You change anything about my circumstances, change me here. Teach me the comfort that comes and stands beside me in the pressure instead of lifting me out of it — and then make me a man who spends it. Let nothing I have suffered be wasted on me. Lord, I confess that I have despaired of my own strength, and I thank You that this was never my failure but Your design. Keep me from trusting in myself. Anchor me in the God who raises the dead. You delivered me, You are delivering me, and I set my hope on You that You will still deliver me. Jesus, I am a clay jar. I have spent years apologising for the cracks and begging You for a better vessel. Today I stop. Put Your treasure in me, and let the exceeding greatness of the power be Yours and never mine. When I am pressed on every side, keep me from being crushed. When I am perplexed, keep me from despair. When I am pursued, remind me that I am not forsaken. When I am struck down, lift my head — because I am not destroyed. Take my eyes off the things that are seen and fix them on the things that are not seen, and teach me to call my affliction light because I have felt the weight of the glory on the other side of the scale. Over every place in me that is fraying, pitch Your tent. Let the power of Christ rest on my weakness. I receive Your word today in its present tense: Your grace is sufficient for me — not one day, not when this is finally over, but now. So I will boast in my weakness. I refuse to keep measuring myself by people You never asked me to be; I lay down the comparison, I lay down the resentment, and I lay down the credentials I have been trying to earn. Let the only commendation I chase be Yours. Holy Spirit, unveil my face, and change me from glory to glory into the image of the One I am looking at. Make me an ambassador who begs people to be reconciled to God, and let the love of Christ press in on me from both sides until I can only move in one direction. Thank You that He who knew no sin was made sin for me, so that in Him I might become the righteousness of God — I did not earn that, and I cannot lose it. Make me a giver who is cheerful and not grudging, who gives himself to the Lord first and to people second. Search me as I read: if there is anything in me that is not in the faith, expose it now while there is mercy on the table. And when I reach the thorn in chapter 12, give me the grace to stop demanding removal and start receiving sufficiency — for when I am weak, then am I strong. Let the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with me through all thirteen chapters of this book. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!
